extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (readers of John Locke)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing ideas of time and space
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and conceptual analysis of the origins and nature of the ideas of duration (time), expansion (space), and number; explains how the mind forms and applies measures (hours, feet, etc.) and contrasts properties of time vs. space. Appropriate for philosophical study and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our Measure of Time applicable to Duration before Time
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind, having once got such a measure of time as the annual revolution of the sun, can apply that measure to durations wherein that measure itself did not exist; we can intelligibly reckon years before the sun or motion existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: saying 'Abraham was born in year X of the Julian period' is intelligible even if the sun did not exist then. Analogy: applying a foot or yard to distances beyond the world. Emphasises that measures are ideas applied by thought, not dependent on real co-existence of the measuring motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: We can measure space in thought where there is no body
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as we apply measures of time to durations before motion, we can apply measures of length (miles, feet) in thought to spaces where no bodies exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: imagining 5639 miles to the remotest body is like imagining 5639 years before the first existence of any body. The idea is that mental application of a measure does not require the real existence of the referent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of assuming the world is neither boundless nor eternal
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of illustrating ideas of time and space, it is permissible to suppose the world is finite in duration and extension; such suppositions are conceivable and usable in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes it's not necessary to prove finitude here, only that one may legitimately suppose it to explore beginnings of motion and bounds of bodies; the limits of space and duration are beyond full comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternity as an idea formed from measures of duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Having ideas of succession and duration, and being able to add repeated measures of duration indefinitely, we form the idea of eternity as unbounded continuation of duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: adding minutes/hours/years repeatedly 'in infinitum' produces the notion of eternity. Example: measuring a past candle-flame by imagining how a sundial's shadow would have moved if the sun had existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of Duration depend on our ideas (not on co-existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions like hour, day, or year are ideas of lengths of periodical motions; because these are ideas in memory/ reflection, we can apply them to durations antecedent to any actual motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that measuring a past duration only requires a clear idea of the length of some periodical motion, not the real co-existence of that motion with the measured event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of something need not co-exist with the motion we measure it by
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure duration it is not requisite that the measured thing co-existed with the periodic motion used as a standard; we can imagine different historical reckonings equally intelligibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: different cultures' reckonings of the world's age (Egyptian, Chinese) are equally imaginable and comparable even if their reference motions didn't exist then. The capacity to imagine different durations comes from having the idea of periodic lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity in Duration (idea of endless addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: By considering a small unit of duration and repeatedly adding it, the mind can proceed to infinity; this process gives us our notion of eternity, analogous to infinity of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: adding minutes until one reaches an hour and continuing indefinitely. The idea of eternity is derived from the capacity to add measures without end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of our ideas of duration and its measures (sixfold account)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas of duration and measures of it arise from two sources: reflection and sensation, summarized in six steps (succession, distance in succession, periodic sensations, ability to repeat measures mentally, adding measures to form eternity, and considering parts to form general time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six points are: (First) observing train of ideas yields idea of succession; (Second) observing distance between parts of succession yields idea of duration; (Third) sensation of regular appearances yields measures (minutes/hours/days); (Fourth) repeating such measures mentally yields imagining durations without real existence; (Fifth) adding measures indefinitely yields idea of eternity; (Sixth) considering parts of infinite duration as set out by measures gives the general idea of Time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both duration and expansion capable of greater and less
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration (time) and expansion (space) are both ideas of continued lengths and are each capable of being greater or lesser; we can clearly distinguish an hour from a day as readily as an inch from a foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses this comparison to motivate examining the two together for clearer conception; 'expansion' used to avoid material connotations of 'space'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion (space) not bounded by matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can extend the idea of spatial length beyond the limits of bodies by repeating an idea of a unit length, and thus conceive expansion without end, not stopped by matter's bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between arriving at bounds of solid extension (body) and the mind's capacity to conceive endless expansion; invokes theological remark that God is not confined to matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration is not bounded by motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly to expansion, the mind can extend ideas of duration beyond existence of corporeal beings or motions; one can conceive boundless duration not limited by the lifetime or motions of bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that duration can be made 'boundless' though every one admits that God 'fills eternity'; counters that we shouldn't limit ideas of duration to motions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explains why people more readily admit infinite duration than infinite expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: People more readily conceive infinite duration because they attribute duration to God, whereas extension is commonly attributed only to matter; thus they doubt extension without matter but not duration without bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological/sociolinguistic observation: words and attributions direct thought; people more easily imagine eternity than immensity without matter because of how the concepts are commonly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time:Duration :: Place:Expansion (analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time (as a determinate portion of duration) corresponds to place (as determinate portion of expansion); both are parts distinguished by landmarks (motions or bodies) and used to situate finite beings in boundless duration/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that without fixed points or periods distinguishing parts, order of finite things would be lost in boundless expansion or duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'time' and 'place' (co-existent and designed-by-measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: First sense: time/place as that portion which is measured by and co-existent with motions/bodies (begins/ends with sensible world). Second sense: time/place as portions we designate by measures taken from bulk or motion, applied even where real co-existence didn't occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying an event occurred in the Julian period before real days existed; applying measures to imagined portions of the infinite. Makes explicit the flexibility of these terms in discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where and When belong to finite existences
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions 'where' and 'when' make sense only for finite beings and are always reckoned from known parts of the sensible world; they are tools for situating finite existences within infinite duration/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains measurement of position and duration for finite things uses preconceived ideas (inches, feet, minutes, years) and fixed points known to us.

rubrics_metrics.name: All parts of extension are extension; all parts of duration are duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Both expansion and duration are composed of parts all of the same kind; although treated among simple ideas, none of the distinct ideas of either are without composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that mind cannot frame an idea of indivisible space; the smallest familiar measures (span, pace, minute) serve as simple units in thought; both are divisible/ addable in infinitum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of expansion and duration are inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Although parts of bodies or motions may be interrupted (rest, sleep), the conceptual parts of expansion and duration are not separable even in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to underscore the unity and continuity of the conceptual 'parts' despite interruptions in the sources of measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration as a line; Expansion as a solid (difference in structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration is like a straight line (one-dimensional, successive), whereas expansion is capable of multiplicity of directions (figure, breadth, thickness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to differences in conceivability: duration's parts succeed one another and cannot coexist; expansion's parts coexist. Raises question of how spirits/angels relate to expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration has never two parts together; Expansion's parts exist together
rubrics_metrics.description: No two parts of duration exist simultaneously (they are successive), while parts of expansion (space) exist together and are not successive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses this to compare finite beings' experience of time with divine eternity (God's knowledge/perception of all times); implies experiential asymmetry between finite beings and God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number as the simplest and most universal idea (unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of unity ('one') is the simplest and most universal idea, present with every object or thought; number applies to anything that exists or can be imagined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivates why number is foundational and ubiquitous in thought; introduces number as a basic simple idea from which complex modes are formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of number formed by addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex numerical ideas arise by repeating and adding the simple idea of unity (one+one=two, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains formation of counting and larger numbers as repeated addition of units; conceptual basis for numeracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each numerical mode is distinct and precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Each numerical mode (e.g., two, three) is clearly distinct from any other; the least variation (one unit) renders a distinct idea, making numerical ideas more determinate than many spatial ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports claim that numerical demonstrations are especially precise, since the difference between adjacent numbers is unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrations in numbers more precise and general
rubrics_metrics.description: Because numerical ideas are clear and distinct, demonstrations in numbers are more precise and widely applicable than demonstrations about extension, where small differences are less discernible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives comparison: 91 is as distinct from 90 as from 9000, whereas in space small excesses are not easily observed; angles and minute spatial differences lack the same discrete clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names are necessary for numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning names (or marks) to distinct numerical collections is essential for counting and retaining ideas of large numbers; without names it's hard to keep precise numerical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains counting as adding units and giving the aggregate a name; lack of names limits peoples' ability to conceive large numbers (example: some American tribes only had words up to small counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and memory constrain numeracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A scant language (few numeral words) and limited memory prevent formation of distinct ideas for large numbers; cultural tools (naming conventions) enable higher numeracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic examples: some peoples lacked names above 5; inability to count to 1000 traced to lack of words and memory for long numeral sequences. Proposes that inventing systematic denominations could extend counting capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for children to learn counting
rubrics_metrics.description: To count successfully, the mind must (1) distinguish two ideas differing by one unit; and (2) retain in memory the names/marks of the sequence in correct order; failure in either prevents progress in numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains developmental observation: children may reason well before they can count; counting requires both discrimination of adjacent cardinalities and memory for the ordered numeral series.
